I would like to ask about something that did not go well. Tell me about a time you failed, and please make it a real one.
In 2022 I promoted my best field engineer to run two sites at once. Six months later he resigned, and one of the sites was eleven weeks late.
Whose decision was the promotion?
Mine, entirely. I misjudged what he wanted. I saw a great engineer and assumed he wanted to manage people. I wish I had asked him.
Why do you think it went wrong? I am asking for the root cause, not the symptoms.
The root cause was that I gave him the title and none of the tools. I regret not training him before the move. He did not fall short. I did.
And what is different on your sites today because of it?
It was a wake-up call. Nobody is promoted now without a conversation first and a ninety-day handover. Two engineers have been promoted that way since, and both are still with us.
The decision was mine, and so was the mistake.
I misjudged what he wanted, and I wish I had asked him.
The root cause was a title with none of the tools behind it.
Now nobody is promoted without a conversation first.

When I ask about a failure, I already know you have one, so I am not testing whether you will admit it. I am testing three things. The first is size. Candidates bring me a tiny failure, a typo in a report or a meeting that started late, because they think a small failure is a safe one. It is the opposite. If the failure was too small to hurt anybody, you have told me that nobody ever trusted you with anything that could go wrong. The second thing is ownership. I listen for the first time you say they, or the client, or the market. One sentence of context is fine. The moment you start shifting the blame, the answer is over, however good the rest of it is. And the third thing, the one that separates the strong answers from the rest, is evidence. Everybody tells me they learned something. Very few can tell me what they do differently now, on an ordinary Tuesday, because of it. A lesson with no change in behavior is a story, not a lesson. And please, do not dwell on it. Say the regret once, and then move on.

The first time somebody asked me for a failure, I gave the answer everybody gives. I said I worked too hard and trusted people too much, and I watched the interviewer stop writing. It was a strength wearing the clothes of a failure, and she had probably heard it forty times that week. The real failure was sitting right there and I did not use it. Two years earlier I had launched a product in a market we did not understand, and it fell short of the target by more than half. The second time I was asked, I owned up to it in the first sentence. I said the root cause was simple: I had never spoken to a single customer before we built it. I said I wished I had spent one week in that market instead of three months in meeting rooms. Then I stopped talking about the regret, and I described the rule we have now. Nobody signs off on a new product until they have interviewed ten customers personally. That rule was the real answer, not the failure.
